deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Riemann's student essay 'Versuch einer allgemeinen Auffassung der Integration und Differentiation' (1847). It was published posthumously in the Werke (1876). He uses Gauss's Π(s) = Γ(s+1). A value of the fractional derivative ∂_x^ν z is defined as the coefficient p_ν in a generalized Taylor expansion z(x+h) = Σ_ν p_ν h^ν/Π(ν), with ν running over ν0 + Z, subject to d p_ν/dx = p_{ν+1}. The page derives an explicit value.

Step 1 (end of previous page). Ordinary Taylor expansion about a base point k: z(x) = Σ_{n≥0} z^{(n)}(k) (x-k)^n/n!.

Step 2. Replace x by x+h. Expand each (x-k+h)^n/Π(n) by formula (3), the generalized binomial: (y+h)^a/Π(a) = Σ_μ [h^μ/Π(μ)] [y^{a-μ}/Π(a-μ)], with μ over a residue class μ0+Z, μ from -∞ to ∞. Collecting powers of h gives
z(x+h) = Σ_μ [h^μ/Π(μ)] · p_μ, where
p_μ = Σ_{n≥0} z^{(n)}(k) (x-k)^{n-μ}/Π(n-μ).
The manuscript's left side reads 'Z(x)'; it should be z(x+h).

Step 3. Since d/dx [(x-k)^a/Π(a)] = (x-k)^{a-1}/Π(a-1), we get d p_{μ-1}/dx = p_μ. So the coefficient of h^μ/Π(μ) is the derivative of the coefficient of h^{μ-1}/Π(μ-1). Hence p_μ is a value of ∂_x^μ z; the red marginal note replaces the notation d^μz/dx^μ by ∂_x^μ z.

Step 4. Differentiate p_μ with respect to k. Each term gives z^{(n+1)}(k)(x-k)^{n-μ}/Π(n-μ) - z^{(n)}(k)(x-k)^{n-μ-1}/Π(n-μ-1). The sum telescopes (my filling), leaving
dp_μ/dk = -z(k) (x-k)^{-μ-1}/Π(-μ-1).
Therefore p_μ = ∫ -z(k)(x-k)^{-μ-1}/Π(-μ-1) dk + const.

Step 5. Fixing the constant. For μ<0 every exponent n-μ is positive, so every term of p_μ vanishes at k = x; thus p_μ = 0 when k = x. Hence p_μ equals the integral of dp/dk taken between x and the base point k: p_μ(k) = ∫_x^k (-z(t))(x-t)^{-μ-1}/Π(-μ-1) dt = (1/Π(-μ-1)) ∫_k^x (x-t)^{-μ-1} z(t) dt.
This is legitimate provided the integrand is integrable. Riemann notes this holds since z is continuous on [k,x] and -μ-1 > -1. The next page states the result as formula (7): the Riemann–Liouville fractional integral of order -μ with lower terminal k.
errors: Left side of the displayed series is written Z(x); by the construction (x replaced by x+h) it must be z(x+h). This is a slip of the pen.

'Das Integral von k bis x genommen' is ambiguous about orientation. With the integrand -z(k)(x-k)^{-μ-1}/Π(-μ-1), the value p_μ results when the integral runs from x to the base point k, equivalently +(1/Π(-μ-1))∫_k^x (x-t)^{-μ-1}z(t)dt. The next page's (7) is consistent with this.

Unjustified steps: (a) the Taylor series and its termwise use need analyticity on [k,x], not mere 'continuity'; Riemann's 'continuirlich' is stronger than modern continuity here; (b) expanding (x-k+h)^n via the doubly infinite generalized binomial series (3) is formal; its convergence is not addressed; (c) termwise differentiation in k and rearrangement of the double series are not justified.
The condition μ<0 is needed both for the vanishing at k=x and for integrability. It is stated only as -μ-1 > -1; the next page makes 'μ negativ' explicit.

results.what: A value of the fractional derivative of order μ<0 is (1/Γ(-μ))∫_k^x (x-t)^{-μ-1} z(t) dt, derived as a coefficient of a generalized Taylor expansion via differentiation with respect to the base point k
results.modern_name: Riemann–Liouville fractional integral (with arbitrary lower terminal)
results.usually_credited_to: Abel (1823) / Liouville (1832) for related forms; the lower-terminal form is named Riemann–Liouville after this 1847 Riemann essay (published 1876)

results.what: Generalized Taylor series z(x+h) = Σ_μ ∂^μ z(x) h^μ/Γ(μ+1) over μ in μ0+Z, with coefficients p_μ = Σ_n z^{(n)}(k)(x-k)^{n-μ}/Γ(n-μ+1)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1847, publ. 1876); later Hardy, Watanabe, Osler

deep.surprise_reason: This page is part of Riemann's well-known 1847 essay on fractional calculus, printed in his Werke. It is the very source of the name 'Riemann–Liouville integral', so the content is already credited to him.

checkable.asserts: Termwise k-derivative of p_μ for z=exp, which telescopes to -z(k)(x-k)^{-μ-1}/Γ(-μ); should give 0
p_μ series equals the Riemann–Liouville integral (1/Γ(-μ))∫_k^x (x-t)^{-μ-1}z(t)dt for z=exp, μ=-1/2; result ≈ 0
Riemann–Liouville integral of order α=-μ of t^a with k=0 gives Γ(a+1)/Γ(a+α+1) x^{a+α}, consistent with ∂_x^μ x^a = Π(a)/Π(a-μ) x^{a-μ}
d/dx[(x-k)^s/Π(s)] = (x-k)^{s-1}/Π(s-1), which gives d p_{μ-1}/dx = p_μ

transcription_corrections: The base point is written with a capital K in the manuscript (K, Z_K, dK), not lowercase k.
Left side reads 'Z(x)=' as transcribed, but mathematically z(x+h) is meant (Riemann's slip).
In 'ein Werth von [-d-] d^μz/dx^μ' the struck-out red-corrected symbol is replaced by ∂_x^μ z per the red marginal note; the placeholder struck out before 'p_μ' looks like a φ/ψ, as transcribed.
'(d^2z/dx^2)_{(k)}' terms: the manuscript shows stray struck marks after the derivative subscripts (e.g. after (dz/dx)_(k) a struck '(k)' or '(x)'); these are deletions, not factors.
